match.reason: No bank point teaches depreciation as a fixed amount per unit of use: the declining balance card uses a fixed percentage of current value, and the accounting depreciation card is a broader general treatment of spreading cost over useful life.

draft.title: Unit cost depreciation
card: Some assets lose value because of how much they are used, not how long they are owned. Unit cost depreciation takes off a fixed amount for each unit of use, such as each kilometre driven or each hour a machine runs.
Depreciation = cost per unit × number of units used. Value after use = purchase price − depreciation.
Example: a van costs $40 000 and depreciates by $0.20 per km. After 60 000 km, depreciation = 0.20 × 60 000 = $12 000. The value is 40 000 − 12 000 = $28 000.
The value falls by the same amount for each unit used. If the asset is not used in a year, it does not lose value that year.
draft.remember: Unit cost depreciation: value = purchase price − (cost per unit × units used).

a.q: A delivery truck costs $90 000 and depreciates by $0.30 per km. What is its value after 50 000 km?
a.why: Depreciation = 0.30 × 50 000 = $15 000. The value is 90 000 − 15 000 = $75 000. The $15 000 option is the depreciation, not the value left.
a.clue: Find the amount lost first, then take it from the price.

b.q: Priya's printing press cost $24 000. It depreciates by $0.05 per page printed. It has printed 200 000 pages and is not in use this month. What is its value now?
b.why: Depreciation = 0.05 × 200 000 = $10 000, so the value is 24 000 − 10 000 = $14 000. Time spent idle adds no depreciation, because this method depends only on use. The $10 000 option is the amount lost, not the value.
b.clue: Only pages printed count, not the months passed.
